newsitem.title: ANGOLA: UNITA military chiefs prepare for Angolan peace.
newsitem.headline: UNITA military chiefs prepare for Angolan peace.

text.p: Five Angolan former rebel leaders waiting to be absorbed into a new national army are the most protected men in the government-controlled capital of Luanda.
Heavily armed police in blue uniforms guard them round the clock at a luxury hotel as they await service alongside troops from the MPLA government they fought for two decades.

According to a peace pact both sides signed in 1994, the former rebel UNITA military chief General Arlindo Chenda Ben Ben will now become deputy to the government army's chief of staff, General Joao de Matos.
Waiting with Ben Ben in high-security luxury are four other UNITA generals.
But despite the pieces of paper, the peace process is not running smoothly and Ben Ben knows how wrong it can go.
It will be the second time in five years that the 37-year-old will join former war rivals in a single army.

In 1992, he and 300 UNITA troops, taken into the state army during a brief peace, fought their way out of Luanda behind UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi after he rejected elections won by his MPLA (Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola) rival, Jose Eduardo dos Santos.
"Personally, I always wanted to stay (in Luanda) but every time that I have left it was because I was forced to," Ben Ben told Reuters in an interview.
The ensuing three years of war in Angola were more vicious than before. Thousands of people died from starvation and fighting, while others fled their villages.
Ben Ben and the four other generals arrived in Luanda again on September 9. Four more are due to arrive later this month to proceed with military integration.
Under a similar political process, Savimbi was meant to become President dos Santos' deputy but last month rejected the job, throwing a spanner in the peace timetable.

Western diplomats say he will settle for nothing less than becoming president of Angola and without that prospect prefers to lead UNITA (National Union for the Total Independence of Angola) from its northern base in Bailundo.
Ben Ben said he and army leader de Matos get on well.

"We understand that each one had to defend the politics of his party...but when we have met there is an understanding and at the same time we tell historic stories from the war and there are no problems.
"What happened in 1992 was not because of tense personal relations between us," Ben Ben said.
He said there was no outright winner in Angola's war, although he believed UNITA was ahead before the signing of the first peace accord in 1991.
"In May 1991 our president (Savimbi) called me to say we should stop fighting because there was a political avenue that could be a solution," he said.
"At the time we were at our strongest militarily but the political discussions decreased our impetus."
The UNITA military chief admitted it was difficult to return to government territory, saying: "Fear is a human characteristic. It is not easy to flee Luanda."
He said the most difficult part of the Lusaka Peace agreement was the disarming of UNITA guerrillas.
Ben Ben said UNITA would integrate a previously agreed 26,300 soldiers into the new army, but needed help for others who wanted to return to civilian life.
"Integration is voluntary. We have to study what is going to happen to those that will not be integrated because after all these years of war we cannot give them $50 and say 'bon voyage'," he said.
